title: AWS SQS Basics
description: Understand AWS Simple Queue Service, including standard queues, FIFO queues, and message processing patterns.

data.text: Amazon Simple Queue Service (SQS) is a fully managed message queuing service that enables you to decouple and scale distributed systems. It offers two queue types: standard queues for maximum throughput and at-least-once delivery, and FIFO queues for exactly-once processing and strict ordering.

Standard queues are the default type in SQS. They offer nearly unlimited throughput, best-effort ordering, and at-least-once delivery. Duplicate messages are possible, so your consumers should be idempotent. Standard queues are ideal for high-volume workloads like event logging, task processing, and microservice communication where occasional duplicates are acceptable.

FIFO queues guarantee that messages are processed exactly once and in the order they were sent. They have a throughput limit of 300 messages per second (or 3,000 with batching). The queue name must end in .fifo, and each message requires a MessageDeduplicationId or MessageGroupId for ordering. Use FIFO queues when order and uniqueness matter, such as financial transactions or inventory updates.

data.title: FIFO Throughput Limits
data.text: FIFO queues cap at 300 messages per second per queue. Use batching (SendMessageBatch) or multiple message groups to scale. Exceeding limits causes throttling.
Sending and Receiving with the AWS SDK

data.title: Publishing to an SQS FIFO Queue (Node.js)
data.content: The AWS SDK v3 SendMessageCommand sends messages to SQS. FIFO queues require the MessageGroupId parameter.

data.text: When a consumer receives a message, it becomes invisible to other consumers for the visibility timeout period (default 30 seconds). If the consumer fails to delete the message before the timeout, it reappears in the queue for reprocessing. Dead-letter queues (DLQs) capture messages that exceed the maximum receive count, enabling later investigation and replay.

data.title: Long Polling
data.text: Always use long polling (WaitTimeSeconds up to 20 seconds) to reduce empty responses and lower costs. Short polling returns immediately with zero or more messages but may generate many empty responses.

data.caption: SQS message lifecycle with visibility timeout and DLQ
data.definition:
flowchart TD
    P[Producer] -->|Send| SQ[SQS Queue]
    SQ -->|Receive| C[Consumer]
    C -->|Process success| DEL[Delete Message]
    C -->|Process failure| VT[Visibility Timeout Expires]
    VT -->|Return to queue| SQ
    SQ -->|Max receives exceeded| DLQ[Dead-Letter Queue]

items.question: When should I use SQS vs RabbitMQ?
items.answer: Use SQS when you want a fully managed service with no infrastructure to operate. Use RabbitMQ when you need complex routing, on-premises deployment, or protocol flexibility beyond HTTP.

items.question: Can I have multiple consumers on a standard SQS queue?
items.answer: Yes. Standard SQS supports multiple concurrent consumers that load-balance messages across them.

items.question: What happens if a message exceeds 256 KB?
items.answer: You must use Amazon S3 Extended Client Library to store the payload in S3 and send only the reference in the SQS message.

data.title: Key Takeaways
points: Standard queues are for high-throughput, at-least-once delivery
FIFO queues guarantee exactly-once processing and strict order
Use long polling to reduce costs and empty responses
Dead-letter queues isolate failed messages for investigation
data.takeaway: SQS removes operational overhead; choose standard or FIFO based on ordering and duplicate tolerance.
